sentences.text: Arcovenator is the only known species in its extinct genus, a theropod dinosaur belonging to the family Abelisauridae.
Like other abelisaurids, this animal possessed short, high skulls with sculpted surfaces, drastically reduced forelimbs, and robust hind limbs.
While initial estimates placed the creature at 5 to 6 meters long, a later 2016 assessment revised the length to 4.8 meters.
The skull roof features a unique diagnostic trait: a central opening that likely housed the pineal gland on a small dome formed by the moderately thick frontal bone.
Ridges on the parietal bones of the skull fuse to form a sagittal crest.
Its teeth are tall, measuring 3 to 5.5 centimeters, and feature small serrations along the inner and outer ridges.
A unique midline opening on the skull roof may have housed the pineal gland, a structure not commonly found in such a prominent position.
Arcovenator escotae represents the most complete and informative find of French abelisaurids since the discovery of Genusaurus.
A single maxilla found at Pourcieux is likely referable to this species based on its proximity in time and space and phylogenetic analysis.
Fossils of Arcovenator were discovered near Pourrières in southeastern France during pre-construction surveys for the A8 motorway.
The holotype — the specimen the species is based on — consists of a braincase, skull fragments, a tooth, a tail vertebra, a tibia, and a fibula found together in fluvial sandstone.
The genus was named by Tortosa and colleagues in 2013, and the specific name Arcovenator escotae was assigned in the same year.
The animal inhabited the Ibero-Armorican island, a large landmass comprising parts of modern-day France, Spain, and Portugal.
The environment featured warm, subhumid climates with marked seasons, where rivers flowed into a perennial lake.
Fossils were found in fluvial sandstone alongside hybodonts, turtles, crocodylomorphs, pterosaurs, sauropods, the ornithopod Rhabdodon, and nodosaurids.
The abundance of fragmentary remains, especially teeth, suggests that medium-sized abelisaurids like Arcovenator were relatively common in the landscape.
European abelisaurs are divided into a basal lineage and a derived lineage including the larger Arcovenator, which is allied with Majungasaurus and Rajasaurus.
Arcovenator is classified as a theropod genus within the family Abelisauridae.
Researchers named the subclade containing Arcovenator as Majungasaurinae.
Arcovenator lived during the Late Cretaceous period, specifically between 74 and 72 million years ago.
The fossils date to between 72 and 76 million years ago in the Aix-en-Provence Basin of southeastern France.
The animal lived during the Campanian to Maastrichtian stages, from 83.6 to 66 million years ago.
It is debated how European abelisaurs arrived in Europe, with vicariance suggested for older lineages and oceanic dispersal likely for the more recent derived lineage including Arcovenator.
It is debated whether the phylogenetic tree of Abelisauridae and the classification of genera into subgroups remain stable as new data and analysis techniques are applied.
